analysis.one_liner: Banned bank overdraft and bounced-check fees during federal disasters and 120 days after.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred overdraft and nonsufficient fund fees during the COVID-19 emergency, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During any federally declared disaster — starting with COVID-19 — banks would have been barred from charging overdraft and nonsufficient fund fees on checking accounts, or reporting a customer's overdrafts to credit bureaus. The fee ban would last through the emergency plus 120 days. The bill never left the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking-account customers who overdraw their accounts — disproportionately low- and moderate-income households — would have kept money they now pay in fees. The bill's own findings describe flat fees charged on small transactions, multiple fees in a single day, and daily fees while an account stays negative [S3]. All consumers in a disaster area would have been protected, and their overdraft use could not have been reported to credit bureaus, protecting credit scores [S3].

how_it_helps.text: During a covered period, no depository institution could assess a nonsufficient fund fee or an overdraft coverage fee on any transaction — ATM withdrawals, one-time debit card purchases, checks, or automatic recurring payments [S2] [S3].

Banks would also have been barred from reporting negative overdraft information to credit reporting agencies during a covered period, so an overdrawn account could not damage a customer's credit record [S2] [S3].

The protection was not limited to COVID-19: it would apply automatically in any federally declared major disaster or nationwide emergency, ending 120 days after the incident period, and in state-specific disasters it would cover residents of the affected state or tribe [S3].
If a bank charged a banned fee anyway, it would be deemed in compliance only by promptly reversing it, giving customers a direct remedy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Depository institutions — banks, credit unions, and other insured deposit-takers — would lose overdraft and nonsufficient fund fee revenue for the duration of the emergency plus 120 days. Customers might also see banks decline to cover overdrafts, since the bill lets banks keep discretion to pay an overdraft without a fee but does not require them to [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require banks to keep covering overdrafts — it only bars the fees. A bank could respond by simply declining transactions it once covered, leaving customers with declined payments instead of covered ones [S3].

Overdraft coverage is short-term credit that banks extend at a loss when they pay a transaction; eliminating the fee for the covered period removes the bank's revenue for that service, and some institutions might respond with new account fees or by closing accounts of customers who frequently overdraw [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real but temporary: fee-paying customers, mostly lower-income households, would keep their money during an emergency when income is most disrupted, and their credit records would be shielded. The main cost falls on banks, for whom overdraft fees are a large, steady revenue stream. The design risk is that banks could stop covering overdrafts altogether rather than absorb the loss, converting a fee problem into a declined-payment problem. On balance it is a consumer-protection measure whose costs fall on an industry, not on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on April 21, 2020, about a month into the COVID-19 national emergency, with Rep. Carolyn Maloney joining as the original cosponsor [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, where it remained with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action [S1] [S5].
Thirteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with the bill still pending in committee, so it expired without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and other depository institutions are better off: they continued collecting overdraft and nonsufficient fund fees from customers throughout the pandemic emergency, because the bill never received committee or floor action.

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to suspend overdraft and nonsufficient fund fees during the COVID-19 emergency and future disasters

for.name: Rep. Carolyn Maloney
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's original cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Maxine Waters)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in its action history

against.name: House Republican conference
against.what_they_did: None of the 197 House Republicans cosponsored the bill

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats out of 231, with no Republican support recorded; the bill died in a committee led by a Democratic chair without a vote, so its defeat is best described as inaction by the majority rather than a party-line roll call.

industries.note: Overdraft and nonsufficient fund fees are a major, recurring revenue stream earned mostly from customers with low balances; the bill would have cut that revenue during emergencies. The bill's own findings describe banks steering customers into the most expensive flat-fee overdraft option and stacking multiple fees in a day [S3].

Banks would have been barred from reporting overdraft use to credit bureaus during a covered period, temporarily shrinking one category of negative data supplied to them. The effect on the industry is small compared with the effect on banks.
